title: Mark Twain and the Tax Bureau: Literary Wit and Civic Candor
summary: Mark Twain’s famous open letter to the American tax collector, turning a bureaucratic demand into a masterpiece of satirical humor and honest civic reflection.
keywords: Historical Dialogue 136: தமிழ்நாடு சட்டமன்றத்தில் மின்சாரமும் மனைவியும்
full_text:
In 1869, while residing in Hartford, Connecticut, the celebrated American author and humorist Mark Twain received a stern official notice from the local Internal Revenue assessor.

The letter was stiff and bureaucratic:
"Mr. Samuel L. Clemens (Mark Twain),
You have failed to declare your complete earnings derived from literary publications and public lectures over the past fiscal year. You are required to submit an exact accounting of your taxable income immediately, under penalty of statutory enforcement."

Rather than filing an ordinary appeal, Twain picked up his fountain pen and drafted an open response that became a classic of satirical literature:

"Dear Sir,
Your communication has reached me, and I admire your relentless zeal. You ask for a declaration of my true income. A writer's genuine wealth, as any philosopher knows, consists of the laughter he gives to his countrymen and the honest truths he dares to utter. Unfortunately, your revenue tables do not yet accept chuckles as legal tender.

If you insist upon cold cash: I earned a moderate sum by hard labour, but my expenses in purchasing blank paper, ink, and midnight coffee to endure the world's madness nearly exceeded the receipts. However, as a patriotic citizen who wishes to see the republic flourish, I am prepared to be generous. My chief remaining assets consist of a pair of spectacles with one cracked lens and three unwritten plots. I gladly assign fifty percent of each to the United States Treasury!"

The tax assessor was thoroughly disarmed by Twain’s brilliance. Twain promptly paid his lawful assessment in full, demonstrating that civic duty and sparkling wit can walk hand in hand.
